title: The Clock Above Track Four
text:
On the first Monday after the old rail station reopened as a community market, Mara arrived before sunrise to unlock the side doors. The platforms no longer served passenger trains, but the roof still held the iron clock that had faced Track Four for nearly eighty years. Its hands had stopped at 6:17 sometime during the building’s long closure.

The renovation committee had argued about the clock for months. A contractor offered to replace it with a bright digital display that would show the time, market announcements, and emergency messages. The new display would be easier to maintain and could be read from across the hall. Mara understood the reasons. She had spent enough mornings resetting temperamental lights and tightening loose door handles to appreciate equipment that simply worked.

Still, whenever she crossed the hall, her eyes went to the old clock. Her grandfather had once sold newspapers at the station kiosk, and in family stories he always seemed to be checking that clock before the first train. Mara did not believe the clock was valuable merely because it was old. The station had once contained drafty waiting rooms and cracked benches that nobody had wanted to preserve. But the clock had been the one object people mentioned when they learned the building would reopen.

During the first market weekend, vendors arranged bread, flowers, repaired bicycles, and jars of honey beneath the high windows. Visitors kept stopping below the clock. Some remembered catching trains there. Others had never seen the station open, yet they photographed the frozen hands and asked why they still read 6:17. By noon, Mara had told the story so many times that she began to hear how odd it sounded: a public building celebrating its return while its most noticeable clock insisted that time had not moved.

The next week, the contractor arrived to measure the wall for the digital display. Mara watched him set his ladder beneath the clock. “We can store the old one,” he said. “Nothing has to be thrown away.” His answer was practical, and that almost made it harder to object. Storage would protect the clock, but it would also turn it into something people had to remember to go looking for.

Mara asked him to wait one day. She called a local clock repairer, who climbed the ladder, opened the metal case, and found less damage than expected. The mechanism needed cleaning, two worn gears, and a new electrical connection. The repair would cost more than a basic wall clock but less than the digital display. It would not show announcements. It would only tell the time.

At the committee meeting that evening, Mara did not make a speech about history. She brought the two estimates and a photograph from opening weekend. In it, three generations of one family stood beneath the clock, all looking upward. “The new screen does more,” she said. “The question is whether we need this spot to do more.” The committee voted to repair the clock and place a smaller information screen near the entrance instead.

Two weeks later, Mara stood alone in the hall while the repairer moved the minute hand forward. The clock clicked, paused, and then claimed the next minute with a sound too small to fill the station but large enough for Mara to hear from below. She smiled, not because the building had been returned to the past, but because one piece of the past had been given a job in the present.

When the doors opened, most visitors walked beneath the clock without looking up. That pleased Mara more than the photographs had. A working clock was no longer an exhibit demanding attention. It had become part of the station again.
